title: Week 22 · Lesson 46: Ophthalmic & ENT Pharmacology — Red Eye, Glaucoma, Otitis, Rhinitis & Medication Safety
html:
PHASE 2 · ADVANCED PHARMACOLOGY

Week 22 — Lesson 46: Ophthalmic & ENT Pharmacology — Red Eye, Glaucoma, Otitis, Rhinitis & Medication Safety

FNP-level goal: Select eye, ear, and upper-airway medication only after identifying whether the presentation is a routine outpatient condition or a threat to vision, airway, neurologic function, or hearing—and teach administration that makes the prescription effective and safe.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate uncomplicated conjunctival symptoms from red-eye emergencies before prescribing drops.
  • Explain the medication classes used in chronic glaucoma care and the importance of adherence and administration technique.
  • Recognize acute angle-closure glaucoma as an emergency rather than a “headache with red eye.”
  • Apply stewardship principles to acute rhinosinusitis and otitis presentations.
  • Use safe counseling for intranasal agents, decongestants, otic medications, and allergic-rhinitis therapy.

Part 1 — Red Eye: Medication Follows the Examination

Red eye may reflect conjunctivitis, dry eye, blepharitis, corneal abrasion, keratitis, uveitis, scleritis, acute angle closure, trauma, chemical exposure, or infection associated with contact-lens use. Ask about pain, photophobia, vision change, discharge, contact lenses, trauma, chemical exposure, headache/nausea, unilateral vs bilateral onset, and systemic disease.

Decreased visual acuity, significant pain, photophobia, corneal opacity, abnormal pupil, contact-lens-associated painful red eye, trauma, chemical injury, severe headache with nausea/vomiting, or suspected herpes eye disease requires urgent ophthalmic/emergency assessment. Do not use an empiric antibiotic drop to make a vision-threatening eye safe.

Part 2 — Conjunctivitis: Not Every Red Eye Needs Antibiotics

Viral, allergic, and bacterial conjunctivitis can overlap. Watery bilateral symptoms with upper-respiratory illness, prominent itching with allergic triggers, and purulent discharge are clues—not standalone diagnoses. Assess contact-lens use, gonococcal risk when relevant, corneal findings, visual acuity, and symptom severity.

Antibiotic ophthalmic therapy should have a clear indication. Explain hygiene, contagion precautions when relevant, contact-lens guidance, warning symptoms, and expected course. A patient with worsening pain or vision should return urgently instead of trying leftover drops from a prior episode.

Part 3 — Never Send Topical Ocular Anesthetic Home for Self-Treatment

Topical anesthetic drops are useful in clinical evaluation but are not appropriate routine take-home pain medication. They can mask worsening injury and impair corneal healing. The FNP must distinguish a tool for examination from a safe outpatient prescription.

Similarly, topical ophthalmic corticosteroids can be beneficial in selected specialist-guided conditions but can worsen or obscure infection and should not be used as a reflex treatment for undifferentiated red eye.

Part 4 — Glaucoma: Pressure Control Protects Vision

Primary open-angle glaucoma is often asymptomatic until visual damage is advanced. Medication classes used to reduce intraocular pressure include prostaglandin analogues, beta blockers, alpha agonists, and carbonic-anhydrase inhibitors. Choice is directed by ophthalmology and patient-specific ocular and systemic factors.

FNP care supports adherence, medication reconciliation, adverse-effect recognition, and access. Ask whether the patient misses doses, cannot aim the bottle, runs out early, experiences shortness of breath or bradycardia, has eye irritation, or has changed systemic cardiovascular medications. Do not stop prescribed glaucoma treatment casually; coordinate promptly with eye care.

Part 5 — Drop Technique Is Part of the Prescription

For chronic eye drops, confirm the patient can instill one drop, avoid touching the tip to the eye, close the eye gently, and use nasolacrimal occlusion when instructed to reduce systemic absorption. If multiple drops are due at once, separate them so one does not wash out the other. Dexterity impairment, tremor, arthritis, low vision, cost, or refill barriers can cause apparent “treatment failure.”

Ask the patient to demonstrate technique when possible. A medication that never reaches the ocular surface cannot lower intraocular pressure.

Part 6 — Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma: A Vision Emergency

Acute angle closure can present with sudden blurred vision, severe eye pain/headache, nausea/vomiting, a red eye, a hazy cornea, and abnormal pupil findings. It requires immediate emergency/ophthalmic care. The patient may initially describe “a bad migraine” or “sinus headache,” so visual symptoms and eye findings matter.

Do not delay referral by trialing outpatient drops, treating nausea alone, or assuming that a red eye is conjunctivitis. Emergency treatment and definitive ophthalmic intervention are time-sensitive.

Part 7 — Allergic Rhinitis: Treat the Pattern, Avoid Harmful Workarounds

Allergic rhinitis commonly causes itching, sneezing, rhinorrhea, congestion, and seasonal or exposure-linked symptoms. Management can include allergen reduction, saline, intranasal corticosteroids, antihistamines, and selected adjuncts based on symptoms and comorbidity. Correct intranasal technique improves benefit and can reduce irritation or epistaxis.

Oral sedating antihistamines can impair driving, cognition, and fall safety, especially in older adults or people using other CNS depressants. Medication choice should account for work, age, glaucoma/urinary-retention context, alcohol, and polypharmacy.

Part 8 — Decongestants: Short-Term Symptom Relief, Not Risk-Free

Systemic decongestants can affect blood pressure, heart rate, sleep, anxiety, and urinary symptoms. Topical nasal decongestants can cause rebound congestion when overused. Ask about hypertension, arrhythmia, coronary disease, glaucoma risk, pregnancy, stimulant use, insomnia, and prostate/urinary symptoms before recommending a decongestant.

A patient with persistent congestion needs diagnostic reassessment for allergic, viral, bacterial, structural, medication-related, or other causes—not progressively more decongestant.

Part 9 — Acute Rhinosinusitis: Stewardship Is Clinical Reasoning

Most acute rhinosinusitis is viral. Consider acute bacterial rhinosinusitis when symptoms are severe, persistent without improvement, or worsen after an initial viral improvement pattern. Do not prescribe an antibiotic for every day-three URI with colored mucus.

When antibiotics are appropriate, choose therapy using current guidance, allergy history, pregnancy status, kidney function, recent antibiotic exposure, local resistance, and follow-up reliability. Supportive medication can relieve symptoms but does not automatically shorten viral illness. Severe headache, orbital symptoms, vision change, neurologic signs, altered mental status, or toxic appearance requires urgent escalation.

Part 10 — Ear Complaints: Inspect Before Treating

Ear pain can be caused by acute otitis media, otitis externa, referred dental/TMJ pain, eustachian dysfunction, herpes zoster, foreign body, trauma, or mastoid disease. Examine the canal, tympanic membrane, surrounding skin, hearing, and systemic findings. Otic medication safety depends on the diagnosis and tympanic-membrane status.

For suspected otitis externa, canal findings, pain with tragal/pinna movement, diabetes/immune compromise, and severity guide care. Severe pain, granulation tissue, cranial-nerve findings, or systemic illness in a high-risk patient requires urgent evaluation for invasive disease rather than routine ear drops.

Part 11 — Hearing and Ototoxicity

New unilateral hearing loss, sudden sensorineural hearing loss, vertigo with neurologic signs, severe tinnitus, or facial weakness requires prompt evaluation. Do not assume all “muffled hearing” is cerumen or an uncomplicated middle-ear infection.

Medication review matters: some agents have potential ototoxicity, and aminoglycoside-containing otic products or other ear medications must be chosen with attention to tympanic-membrane integrity and current labeling. Refer when exam findings, hearing change, or treatment response are concerning.

Part 12 — Clinical Case: A Red Eye Is Not “Pink Eye”

A contact-lens wearer has a unilateral red eye, severe pain, photophobia, and reduced vision after sleeping in lenses.

FNP reasoning: this is not routine conjunctivitis. Corneal infection/keratitis is a vision-threatening possibility; urgent ophthalmic evaluation is needed rather than empiric routine drops.

Part 13 — Clinical Case: The “Sinus Infection” With Red Flags

A patient reports facial pressure after five days of URI symptoms and requests an antibiotic. They are afebrile and improving overall.

FNP reasoning: this is more consistent with an uncomplicated viral course than immediate bacterial sinusitis. Provide symptom care, stewardship education, and clear return precautions rather than antibiotics by default.

Part 14 — Clinical Case: Congestion Medication in a High-Risk Patient

A 72-year-old with poorly controlled hypertension, insomnia, atrial fibrillation, and urinary hesitancy asks for an oral decongestant.

FNP reasoning: systemic decongestant adverse effects may be clinically important. Reassess the cause of congestion and choose safer symptom-directed alternatives; do not treat an OTC request as risk-free.

FNP Ophthalmic & ENT Medication Framework

  1. Measure visual acuity and assess eye pain, photophobia, pupil abnormalities, trauma, contact lenses, and systemic symptoms before treating red eye.
  2. Use glaucoma medication support to protect adherence, technique, systemic safety, and access—not to replace ophthalmology.
  3. Reserve antibiotics for a defined bacterial indication and document follow-up/return precautions.
  4. Screen for cardiovascular, neurologic, urinary, sleep, and medication-interaction risks before decongestants or sedating agents.
  5. Examine the ear and consider tympanic-membrane status before choosing otic medication.
  6. Escalate immediately for vision loss, acute angle closure, chemical injury, orbital/neurologic signs, invasive ear disease, or toxic appearance.

High-Yield Summary

Red eye: pain, photophobia, reduced vision, contact-lens risk, trauma, or abnormal pupil requires urgent evaluation.
Glaucoma: chronic drops protect vision only when they are accessible and correctly administered.
Acute angle closure: red eye + severe pain/headache + nausea/vision change is an emergency.
Rhinosinusitis: most cases are viral; use bacterial criteria and stewardship.
Decongestants: assess blood pressure, arrhythmia, insomnia, urinary, glaucoma, and pregnancy context.
Ear complaints: inspect first; high-risk otitis externa and sudden hearing loss require escalation.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Ophthalmic and otic diagnosis, medication selection, antibiotic decisions, glaucoma management, and emergency disposition must follow current guidelines, FDA-approved prescribing information, local scope requirements, and the individual patient’s clinical context.
